title: Block close: reforms
hookLine: Protestants and Catholics both reformed, both failed, both produced saints

lines: SOME WOULD NOT HAVE SAT TOGETHER.
cards: Lay out the faces from this block on a table, like old photographs. A monk with a list of theses for debate. A Dutchman turning back across the ice to pull his pursuer out.
A soldier with a shattered leg reading saints' lives in bed. A nun on a dusty road founding small, poor convents. A man at the stake, praying for a king's eyes to be opened.
A tinker writing in a jail cell. A preacher in a field. Some of them would not have shared a table with each other.
Their churches put each other's people to death. And here they are, on one table, in one story.

teach.b: This block began with a church that needed reform, and with the line: always reforming. It ends with three honest sentences. Both reformed.
Luther, Calvin, Menno Simons and Cranmer pressed for a church grounded in scripture, in the people's own language.
Trent, Ignatius, Teresa and Francis de Sales renewed the Catholic Church from the inside: better trained priests, deeper prayer, gentler pastors.
Both failed. Protestants executed Catholics and drowned Anabaptists. Catholics burned Protestants.
Massacres in Paris, a war that tore Europe apart, kings using faith for power. Christians on each side did things this block could not soften.
Both produced saints. Dirk Willems on the ice. Thomas More keeping his conscience.
Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac feeding the poor. Wesley on horseback, starting the Methodist movement. Bunyan, writing about a burden that rolls away.
And outside Europe, people like Las Casas, Kateri and Richard Allen carrying the same faith into very different lives.

teach.h: SEARCH AND TRY OUR OWN WAYS.
teach.b: The book of Lamentations says: "Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD." The verse says our ways, not theirs.
Some Reformed Christians use a phrase for this: a church reformed, and always being reformed. Catholics speak of the church always in need of purifying.

And in John's Gospel, Jesus prays for his followers "That they all may be one". Some churches today tell this story together more than they used to, Protestants and Catholics admitting their own side's wounds.
That's part of the reform too.

how: Protestant and Catholic churches hold joint services and dialogues, and some have issued shared statements on the Reformation that admit wrongs on their own side.

o: a Catholic book of confessions written for the clergy
a Bible book of grief that says: let us search our ways
a Reformation hymn mourning the burning of martyrs

p: Dirk Willems, Vincent de Paul, Bunyan
let us search and try our ways
reform starts with our own side

s: only one side in the reformations did violence
Protestants and Catholics both killed; Anabaptists suffered at the hands of both.
Catholics also reformed their church in this era
Trent, Ignatius, Teresa and Francis de Sales renewed it from the inside.
no church today tells this story except from its own side
some tell it together more than they used to, admitting their own side's wounds.

games.q: you're telling the story of the reformations to a friend from the other side. how do you sum it up?
o: our side was right, and theirs was wrong.
both reformed, both failed, both produced saints.
it was all politics, and none of it was faith.
games.why: that's how this block closes: both reformed, both failed, both produced saints. some churches today tell it together more than they used to.

practice: Bring to mind one person on the other side of a divide from you: another church, another faith, another politics, another side of a family quarrel.
Hold the person, not their opinions, then think of one thing on your own side that needs reform. If you pray, pray for them by name, and for yourself; if you don't, just wish them good.

wordCard.voice: Lamentations. The book whose line, let us search and try our ways, this block borrows to look honestly at its own reforms, failures, and saints.

carryVoice: Your line: reformed and reforming. Tomorrow a new block begins: the modern church across the world. Day nine hundred fifteen, and a block complete.
